note: AUTHORED RULES, TEXT-MATCHED INSTANCES. Each rule below was walked by hand once against card text and the Core Rules, the same way a combos.json entry is. The cards each rule pairs its anchor with are found by running its `partner` predicate over the pool — nobody walked those pairs one by one. That is a weaker guarantee than combos.json and the UI says so. Never merge these into combos.json. `npm run synergies` prints every rule's whole match list and `npm run synergies -- --match` prints only the fragment each predicate caught; `reviewed` is the date somebody read one end to end. Tokens and the two helper cards are dropped from every list, since they are never in a decklist.

synergies.name: Blue Sentinel doubles any hold effect

excludes.why: "When I hold, return me to my owner's hand" — the second trigger finds him already in hand and does nothing.
returns your Chosen Champion only if the Champion Zone is empty, which the first trigger has already stopped being true.
makes your own non-token units cost 1 more; triggering it twice doubles a drawback.

"When I hold, [Buff] all units here" — the second trigger buffs the same fixed group a second time, and 702.3 ("There can only be one Buff on a Unit at a time") means none of them receives a second buff; it is a no-op, not a bigger one.

synergies.why: Every hold effect you have at Blue Sentinel's battlefield triggers one extra time, and two Sentinels there make it three. The effect need not sit on a unit — a battlefield's own hold trigger counts as yours (R8). One caveat the list cannot express: a trigger whose cost is exhausting its own source, as several legends have, can only be paid once unless you ready that source between the two resolutions.

synergies.name: Red Brambleback doubles any conquer effect

excludes.why: the extra instance lands on the copy that has just left the trash and finds it already in your hand. 385.2 does give every copy sitting in the trash its own trigger — three copies answer one conquer three times, each with its own discard — but that is three copies working, not Red Brambleback doubling one.
you MUST recycle one of your runes — triggering it twice doubles a mandatory cost.
the conquer text is quoted inside the spell and granted to the moved unit; it moves that unit to its base, so a second move does nothing.

"When I'm played and when I conquer, buff me" — a fixed self-target, and 702.3 ("There can only be one Buff on a Unit at a time") means the second execution of the same conquer finds him already buffed and does nothing.

synergies.why: Every conquer effect you have at Red Brambleback's battlefield triggers one extra time, the mirror of Blue Sentinel. [Hunt] counts as a conquer effect (823.1.b), so a Hunt unit conquering there gains its XP twice. Same caveat: a trigger paid by exhausting its own source can only fire once unless you ready it in between.

synergies.name: Skyfall of Areion pays a unit's hold effects out on conquer, and back

partner.textExcludes: When I conquer or hold|When I hold or conquer|\[Hunt|after an attack|excess damage

excludes.why: his hold effect returns him to hand; firing it on a conquer as well only takes him off the board sooner.
"When I conquer a battlefield that was uncontrolled" — that condition cannot be met by holding a battlefield you already control.
his conquer effect needs a unit, a gear and a spell played this turn, and a hold resolves in your Beginning Phase before you have played anything.

synergies.why: While attached, Skyfall reads the equipped unit's hold effects as conquer effects and its conquer effects as hold effects, so a unit that paid on only one of the two scoring routes now pays on both. Effects already keyed to both — [Hunt] and any "When I conquer or hold" — gain nothing and are left out.

synergies.name: Reckoner's Arena fires your conquer effects on a hold

excludes.why: "a battlefield that was uncontrolled" is a non-conquer part of the condition and it is false while you are holding the Arena.
needs a unit, a gear and a spell played this turn; a hold resolves in your Beginning Phase, before you have played anything.

synergies.why: Holding the Arena activates the conquer effects of your units there with no combat at all. The Core Rules use this exact card to define what activating a named trigger means, and they also set the limit this list respects: if any non-conquer part of the condition is unfulfilled, the ability does not go on the chain (383.4.g.1).

synergies.name: Svellsongur gives a unit its own recurring trigger twice

excludes.why: the copied trigger returns him to hand, and the second copy finds nothing on the board to return.
her conquer effect returns her to your hand; a second copy of it has nothing left to do.
the "When I attack" text the predicate caught belongs to the Shadow Clone token quoted inside his card, not to Zed.
"When I'm played and when I conquer, buff me" — the copied trigger targets the same fixed body a second time, and 702.3 caps him at one buff, so the copy is a no-op.
"you may move any number of your token units to this battlefield" has no per-execution cap — one instance already moves the whole army, so a second copy of the same trigger has nothing left to move.

synergies.why: Svellsongur copies the unit's text into its own effect text while attached, and that effect text is granted back to the same unit, so a recurring "When I …" trigger goes on the chain twice. R6 = A: it copies the unit's current text, not a snapshot taken when it attached.

synergies.name: Renata Glasc, Industrialist makes your tokens usable the turn they appear
synergies.why: Units enter exhausted and Gold gear tokens are printed "exhausted"; Renata rewrites how both enter, so the token blocks, moves or pays Power the turn it is made. R25 = A: her replacement beats the card's own "exhausted".

synergies.name: The Grand Plaza turns unit tokens into a win condition
synergies.why: Holding the Plaza with seven units there wins outright, and only token makers put that many bodies on one battlefield. Tokens made at your base still have to walk over, so a card that plays them at the battlefield is worth more than one that does not.

synergies.name: LeBlanc, Everywhere at Once keeps [Temporary] bodies past scoring
synergies.why: [Temporary] is a triggered ability that kills the permanent at the start of its controller's Beginning Phase, before scoring. LeBlanc switches those triggers off at her battlefield, so the bodies are still there when you hold. R10 = A. She only covers her own battlefield, so a token made at your base has to move there first — and the list deliberately leaves out the cards that hand [Temporary] to an enemy permanent, which is removal you would rather keep working.

synergies.name: Fiora, Worthy readies a unit a buff pushes over 5 Might

partner.textMatches: \[Buff\]|[Bb]uff (a|all|another|me|up to|your)|[Gg]ive (me|it|a unit|a friendly unit|another friendly unit|your units)[^.]{0,60}\+\d+ :rb_might:

excludes.why: spends a buff as a cost; it consumes Might rather than granting it.
spends a buff as a cost, same as Wallop — a consumer, not a source.
reacts to a buff by readying the unit; it grants no Might of its own.
reacts to being buffed by readying himself; he grants no Might of his own.

synergies.why: A unit becomes Mighty the moment its Might crosses from under 5 to 5 or more (709), and Fiora readies it for one Order rune. Whether a given buff crosses that line depends on the unit's printed Might, so this lists the Might sources, not a promise.

synergies.name: Fiora, Worthy readies a unit an Equipment pushes over 5 Might
synergies.why: Attaching Equipment raises the unit's Might on the spot, and +2 or more takes a 3-Might body over the Mighty line, which readies it under Fiora. Same caveat as the buff rule: the unit's printed Might decides whether the line is actually crossed.

synergies.name: Jayce, Brilliant Inventor buys back an exhaust ability every turn

excludes.why: "exhaust: Pay any amount of Energy to Add that much rainbow" has no cap per activation (per CLAUDE.md's own Ancient Henge note), so a second activation from the same instant is worth exactly zero — anything the second copy could convert, the first could have converted at once.
"exhaust: Pay any amount of rainbow to Add that much Energy" has no cap per activation, so a second simultaneous activation converts nothing a bigger single payment couldn't already.

synergies.why: The first non-token gear you play each turn readies something else that is exhausted, so an ability whose cost includes exhausting its own source runs a second time that turn. He also un-taps an attacker, which no predicate over card text can find.

synergies.name: Ride the Wind fires a move trigger and leaves the unit ready
synergies.why: An effect moving a unit is a Move (420.1), so it sets off that unit's move triggers, and the triggers of any Equipment attached to it. Ride the Wind readies the unit as well, so the body is still available afterwards. A recall is not a Move (456.1) and would not do this.

synergies.name: Relentless Pursuit moves a unit and hands it an Equipment on the way
synergies.why: The same Move as Ride the Wind, but it can attach an Equipment in the same breath, so the move trigger you want can be bolted on to whichever unit is going.

synergies.name: Windswept Hillock lets a move trigger fire on your own terms
synergies.why: Units at the Hillock have [Ganking], which is short for "I may move to a battlefield from another battlefield" (810.1.b), and that move is a Move (420.1) — so it fires the unit's move triggers and those of any Equipment attached to it, on your turn, without spending a card. The Hillock has no domain, so any legend can run it.

synergies.name: Retreat replays a unit that brings another body with it

excludes.why: the predicate caught "play a non-token gear" in his trigger condition; his play effect readies something, it puts nothing on the board.

synergies.why: Retreat returns a friendly unit to hand as a [Reaction] for one Energy, and replaying it fires its Play Effect again (383.4.a.1). The list is deliberately narrow: it holds the units whose play effect leaves another permanent behind, so the bounce pays for the card. Retreat replays every play effect in the game, which is a fact about Retreat rather than a pairing worth naming.

synergies.name: Pack of Wonders replays a body every turn with no card spent

excludes.why: the predicate caught "play a non-token gear" in his trigger condition; his play effect readies something, it puts nothing on the board.

synergies.why: Exhausting the Pack bounces another friendly gear, unit or facedown card to hand; replaying it fires its play effect again. It costs no card, only the Pack readying up, so unlike Retreat it repeats every turn — and unlike Retreat it can bounce a gear.

synergies.name: Aphelios, Exalted charges you for every Equipment you attach to him
synergies.why: Each attach to Aphelios picks a mode not picked this turn — two ready runes, a channelled rune, or a buff — so the value is per Equipment attached, not per Equipment owned. Re-attaching a piece you already control counts.

synergies.name: Ekko, Recurrent turns a sacrifice outlet into a rune refresh
synergies.why: Ekko's [Deathknell] recycles him to ready your runes, so anything that kills your own unit on demand converts him into Power. He has 5 Might, so the outlets that demand a [Mighty] unit can take him too. Recycling sends him to the bottom of the Main Deck, not the trash (416.1).

synergies.name: Malzahar, Fanatic eats tokens for two Power of any domain
synergies.why: Malzahar's cost is killing a friendly unit or gear, and a token is the cheapest thing you own to feed him — so every token a card makes is two rainbow Power once he is on the board.

synergies.name: Wallop is free the moment you have a buff to spend

partner.textExcludes: spend a buff as an additional cost

excludes.why: reacts to a buff by readying the unit; it creates no buff for Wallop to spend.
reacts to being buffed by readying himself; he creates no buff.

synergies.why: Spending a buff as an additional cost ignores Wallop's Energy cost, so any buff source makes readying a unit cost nothing but the card. Only buffs are spendable, so the "+N Might this turn" half of the list feeds Fiora rather than Wallop; the cards that spend a buff themselves are left out, since they compete for the same counter.

synergies.name: Time Warp runs every once-a-turn trigger a second time

partner.textMatches: [Aa]t the (start of (your|my) Beginning Phase|end of your turn)

synergies.why: The extra turn brings a whole Beginning Phase and a whole end of turn with it, so anything keyed to those fires again — and you score your held battlefields again on the way in.

synergies.name: Gardens of Becoming turns idle units into XP to spend
synergies.why: Every unit standing at Gardens of Becoming can exhaust for 1 XP, so costs that would otherwise wait on conquering and holding get paid by units doing nothing else. Two things the list cannot say. The ability is granted to every unit there, and the controller of an ability is the controller of its source (191.4.a), so an opponent's units at that battlefield feed their own XP the same way. And the exhaust is a real cost: a unit that pays it cannot also Standard Move that turn or pay a second exhaust cost (414.3.a, 414.4), though it keeps occupying the battlefield, and Hold asks for Control rather than for readiness (469.2). The trap on the spending side, which no match list shows: XP is a running balance, not a lifetime total — 730.2 reduces it when you spend, and 824.1.d turns a [Level N] ability Inactive the instant you drop below N. Paying one of these costs can switch off a Level ability you were already relying on.

synergies.name: Blood Rose levels your XP thresholds without conquering
synergies.why: Blood Rose turns each unit you play into 1 XP for 1 Energy, so Level abilities — "While you have N or more XP, this card gains …" (824.1.b.1) — come on from the curve instead of from winning battlefields. The tension the list cannot show: a Level ability goes Inactive the instant your total falls below N (824.1.d), and Blood Rose's own "Spend 3 XP, exhaust: Ready a unit" is one of the things that will drop it.

synergies.name: Sanction turns on a unit's Empowered half without paying for it

excludes.why: reads an ENEMY gear's Empowered state to decide whether to disempower or kill it; nothing on Tomb-Raider Barbara cares about being Empowered herself.

synergies.why: [Empower] is short for "[Cost]: Empower this. Play only if not Empowered" (827.1.c.1), so a unit's Empowered half normally has a printed price. Sanction pays none of it, and does it at Reaction speed. It lasts one turn — Sanction disempowers the unit at end of turn (442.1) — so a static "[Empowered][>] I have +N Might" is a one-turn buff, while a "When I become [Empowered]" trigger has already fired and keeps what it did, and can be fired again next turn once the state has lapsed. One card in the list has a depth the rule does not settle: Kayle, Justified may be Empowered up to three times (441.1.c.1), and whether the end-of-turn disempower strips one instance or all of them is not written anywhere.

synergies.name: Hextech Formula empowers a gear for an exhaust instead of its cost
synergies.why: Each of these gear has a stronger printed mode while it is Empowered, and its own [Empower] ability charges for that — Helm of Suppression asks four Energy and a Calm Power (827.1.c.1). Hextech Formula empowers another gear for an exhaust instead, and Empowered is a state that stays until something disempowers it (441.1.a, 442.1), so the cost is paid once and kept. Hextech Formula enters exhausted, so the first empower comes the turn after it lands (414.4).

synergies.name: Stargazer discounts every spell you replay out of the trash
synergies.why: Flow is short for "You may play this from your trash for its flow cost. Then banish it" (829.1.b), and that cost replaces the base cost at finalization (829.1.c.1). Stargazer takes two Energy off it, to a minimum of one, so the second use of a spell you have already spent is the cheap one. Two limits the list cannot show: the discount is Energy only, and several Flow costs also ask for Power, which Stargazer does not touch; and the spell is banished after the replay (829.1.b.1), so this buys one extra use per copy, not a loop.

synergies.name: Rumble, Scrapper makes every Mech in the list bigger
synergies.why: "Your Mechs have +1 Might (including me)" reads the Mech tag and nothing else, so this is the one predicate in the file that needs no text at all — Mega-Mech is a 7-cost Mech with no rules text and still counts. Rumble also plays a 3 Might Mech token every time he holds, and those tokens are Mechs too, though a token never appears in a list and so never appears here. The list cannot show Experimental Hexplate: it is an Equipment that says "I am a Mech", granting the type to whatever it is attached to rather than carrying the tag itself.

synergies.name: Rumble, Hotheaded gives the whole Mech board Assault
synergies.why: The Fury half of the same tribe: "Your Mechs each have [Assault]" is +1 Might while they are attackers, granted off the tag with no text condition on the Mech itself. Assault only pays inside a Combat, where the Attacker designation exists — walking into an empty enemy battlefield is not an attack — so this rule is worth what the deck's attacks are worth, and nothing on a turn that only holds. His other half is a trap the tag cannot show: "When I conquer, you may recycle another friendly unit to play a Mech from your trash. Reduce its Energy cost by the Might of the unit you recycled" reads as an invitation to feed it the 3 Might Mech token that Rumble, Scrapper plays on every hold — the biggest body in the tribe that costs nothing — and it cannot be done. 185 is one sentence, "Tokens are not cards", and 416.1 defines Recycling as taking "one or more cards from a specific zone", so no token ever pays a recycle. The discount has to be bought with a real printing. Killing a token is a different action and does work, which is what `blood-money-small-token-fodder` and `malzahar-token-fodder` are about.

synergies.name: Karthus, Eternal makes every death trigger twice

excludes.why: "[Deathknell] — Recycle me to ready your runes" is a Cost linked to an Effect (202). The first instance recycles Ekko out of the trash; on the second the recycle is impossible, and 203.3 says a player who cannot pay the Cost does not execute the linked Effect. The extra trigger readies nothing.

The Zero Drive's granted "[Deathknell] — Banish me" moves the dead unit out of the trash once. The second instance finds nothing left to banish, so it is a no-op — and The Zero Drive's payoff counts units banished with it, not times it tried.

synergies.why: "Your [Deathknell] effects trigger an additional time" reads a characteristic the rules make referenceable (808.3), so every Deathknell on your board resolves twice: two Recruit batches off Machine Evangel, two runes channeled off Soaring Scout, two units back from the trash off Glasc Mixologist. Two things the list cannot say. The doubling copies the whole effect including its downside — Undercover Agent becomes discard 4 then draw 4, Kog'Maw deals 4 twice to every unit at his battlefield including yours — and drawing more is a liability in a game with Burn Out (431.1.a). And 808.1.d.1 removes the trigger entirely if the death is replaced by a recall, so a Zhonya's Hourglass or a heal-and-recall effect turns both instances off at once, not one.

synergies.name: Bandle Tree banks a second facedown card at the same battlefield
synergies.why: A Facedown Zone holds exactly one card (107.3.b) and Bandle Tree is the pool's way of raising that maximum (107.3.b.1), so the battlefield that would bank one trick banks two. What each card is worth there is 811.6: a hidden card gains Reaction while facedown, so it comes back on any player's turn for the [Hidden] price instead of its printed cost — Fox-Fire, Hidden Blade and Hostile Takeover are the expensive end of that. The predicate keys on the reminder text rather than on the bracket, because the keyword itself is printed without brackets on Windsinger (a registered upstream anomaly), and because six cards in the pool name [Hidden] while carrying none — Ava Achiever, Swift Scout, Guerilla Warfare, Ember Monk, Noxus Saboteur and Mystic Vortex all read the keyword on other cards. The cost the list cannot show: 107.3.d removes every facedown card there during the next Cleanup if you lose control of the battlefield, so Bandle Tree doubles the exposure along with the storage.

synergies.name: Trapping Grounds pays for the attacking Might you could not assign
synergies.why: R28 ruled that "excess damage" is attacking Might that never got assigned, because 465.2.c.4 forbids giving a unit more damage than the minimum needed to kill it. [Assault] is the pool's printed way to add Might that only exists while attacking (807.1.c), and 807.2 sums every source, so Assault is the cheapest route to the three excess damage Trapping Grounds asks for — and to the same clause on Yeti Brawler, Piltover Enforcer, Tryndamere and Sivir, Ambitious. Two things the list cannot say. Assault pays nothing outside a Combat: the Attacker designation only exists when a garrison is there to fight (383.4.e, 807.1.d), so walking into an empty enemy battlefield conquers without generating a point of excess. And three of the matches carry the Assault inside a quoted token ability rather than on themselves — both Zeds and Death Mark hand it to a Shadow Clone — which still lands on your board and still counts, unlike the nested quotes that are false positives elsewhere in this file.

synergies.name: Shadow Temple fills the trash these cards spend
synergies.why: Every turn you hold there, Shadow Temple puts three cards from your Main Deck into your trash for nothing — the only repeatable free trash filler in the pool — and the trash is where [Flow] spells are cast from, where Soulgorger and The Harrowing find a body, and what Vi, Garbage Grabber, Assembly Rig and Last Rites pay their costs with. The predicate is deliberately one-directional: it catches cards that take something OUT of your trash, not the other burn and discard effects that only put cards in, because two fillers are not a pair. The cost, which no match list shows: 431.1.b makes putting cards from your Main Deck into the trash in excess of what remains a Burn Out, so holding this battlefield is a self-imposed clock, and Forge of the Future's "Recycle up to 4 cards from trashes" is on the list precisely as the answer to it. Two matches are subtler than they look. Hallowed Tomb returns your Chosen Champion from the trash, and 103.2.a.3 makes every same-named copy in your Main Deck count as that Chosen Champion, so a Burn 3 really can put one there. And Dr. Mundo is on the list for a clause that is a drawback, not a payoff — "At the start of your Beginning Phase, recycle 3 from your trash" empties the very pile his Might is counted from; Shadow Temple refills exactly what he is forced to give back.

synergies.name: Ezreal, Prodigy halves every Accelerate cost
synergies.why: 805.2 calls Accelerate "an Optional Additional Cost" in those words, and Ezreal is the only card in the pool that makes optional additional costs cheaper, so he cuts the one printed exception to "units enter exhausted" in half. What that exception is worth: 359.2.c lets you choose the location a unit is played to, so Accelerate is not about presence — it is about acting. 143.4 enters the unit exhausted and 143.4.a names Accelerate as the way to alter that, while 144.2 makes exhausting the unit the cost of a Standard Move, so an ordinary unit can neither move nor pay an exhaust cost on the turn it lands. That is why Riot printed Accelerate almost entirely on attack and move payoffs: five of the twenty-six carry [Assault], four have a "When I move" trigger and two have "When I attack". Three things the list cannot say. The discount is 1 Energy OR 1 rainbow, never both, and 805.1.a.1 restricts the Power half to a domain the unit itself has, so an accelerated unit is never free — it drops to one rune of its own domain, or to one Energy. Ezreal's reduction is generic, so a deck holding him also pays less for [Repeat] (820.1) and for every "you may pay X as an additional cost" clause; this list is the narrow half of what he does. And this is the only pairing the keyword can have at all: 805.3 says outright that "Accelerate has no function while on the board", 805.2.a forbids paying it once the unit is there and 805.4 makes a second instance redundant, so no card can read it off a permanent the way Renata Glasc, Industrialist reads a token entering. The interaction has to happen at the moment of payment, and Ezreal is the only card standing there.

synergies.name: Dark Child pays for a Reaction spell on the opponent's turn

excludes.why: the [Reaction] is inside the quoted text of the Gold token it makes, not the spell's own speed; Deadly Flourish itself is played at normal speed.

synergies.why: 415.3.a readies your objects during the Awakening Phase on their turn, so a rune you exhausted on your own turn is dead for the whole of the opponent's. Dark Child hands two of them back at end of turn, 167 empties the Rune Pool and not the runes, and 164.2.a's "[E]: [Reaction] - Add [1]" turns them into resources at Reaction speed. What that buys is this list: 813.1.c.1 makes a Reaction card playable during Closed States on any player's turn. Only the spells are listed — a Reaction ability on a permanent you already control is paid the same way, but the pairing worth naming is the card you could not otherwise cast. Her identity is Fury/Chaos, so a deck only ever sees the Fury and Chaos end of the list.

synergies.name: Azir, Sovereign carries tokens stranded at your base to a battlefield

excludes.why: its own reminder says the four Recruits "can be played to your base or to battlefields you control", so it never strands them and needs no relay.

synergies.why: Points are scored at battlefields and 355.2.a defaults a token to your base, where 143.4 leaves it exhausted and 420.3.a charges an exhaust for the Standard Move it can no longer pay. Azir moves any number of your token units by effect (420.2.a), which pays neither that cost nor 144.4's destinations. He is the only card in the pool that does it in bulk. His trigger is "When I attack", so it needs a real Combat: entering an empty enemy battlefield gives no Attacker designation and never fires it. Three of the seventeen print a ready token, and there the relay saves the exhaust the Standard Move would have cost rather than the whole walk.

synergies.name: Forgotten Signpost walks an exhausted token over for nothing

excludes.why: its own reminder says the four Recruits "can be played to your base or to battlefields you control", so it never strands them and needs no relay.

synergies.why: The same bottleneck as Azir's, solved one body at a time and at [Action] speed for 0 Energy and 0 Power: the cost is exhausting a unit you already have at the destination plus the gear itself. Because it is a move by effect (420.2.a) it skips 420.3.a's exhaust and 144.4's destination list, which is exactly what a token needs — 143.4 makes it enter exhausted and 355.2.a leaves it at your base. Three of the seventeen print a ready token, and there the relay saves the exhaust the Standard Move would have cost rather than the whole walk.

synergies.name: Blood Money eats a small token of yours for two Gold

excludes.why: the Bird token is played by an opponent you choose, so Blood Money pays one Gold for it instead of two, and its [Deflect] charges you a rainbow to choose it at all.

synergies.why: Blood Money kills a unit at a battlefield with 2 Might or less, and pays double for a friendly one: two Gold gear tokens against an enemy's one. The list is the token makers whose printed Might fits under that cap. Two cautions ride with it. The body has to be at a battlefield, not at your base, which is the walk the Azir and Forgotten Signpost rules pay for. And UNL-077 Soul Shepherd, "Your token units have +1 Might", pushes a Sand Soldier from 2 to 3 and out of range — it is anti-synergy here, not a partner. R25 = A: with Renata Glasc, Industrialist on the board the two Gold enter ready and are Power the same turn instead of the next.

synergies.name: Defender of Tomorrow buys back a gear's exhaust ability every turn

excludes.why: its only exhaust ability is "Kill this" — after one use the gear is in the trash, where no ready can reach it.
the ability's cost is "Kill this", so the gear is gone by the time it is exhausted; readying it buys nothing.
same shape — "Kill this, 1 Energy, exhaust" puts it in the trash on its only activation.
its exhaust ability hands the gear to a player of your choice and recalls it; a second use is not yours to have, and it is no longer a friendly gear.

"exhaust: Pay any amount of Energy to Add that much rainbow" has no cap per activation (per CLAUDE.md's own Ancient Henge note), so a second activation from the same instant is worth exactly zero — anything the second copy could convert, the first could have converted at once.
"exhaust: Pay any amount of rainbow to Add that much Energy" has no cap per activation, so a second simultaneous activation converts nothing a bigger single payment couldn't already.

synergies.why: "1 Energy, exhaust: Ready a gear", and two of them once Empowered, so any gear whose ability costs its own exhaust runs a second and third time in the same turn. 415.1 only marks an object already on the board, which is why the four gear whose ability kills or gives away their own source are left out. He is a legend, so this rule only ever fires for a Mind/Body list — he is the pool's only legend in that pair.

synergies.name: Veiled Temple readies a gear each time it changes hands

excludes.why: its only exhaust ability is "Kill this" — after one use the gear is in the trash, where no ready can reach it.
the ability's cost is "Kill this", so the gear is gone by the time it is exhausted; readying it buys nothing.
same shape — "Kill this, 1 Energy, exhaust" puts it in the trash on its only activation.
its exhaust ability hands the gear to a player of your choice and recalls it; a second use is not yours to have, and it is no longer a friendly gear.

synergies.why: "When you conquer here, you may ready a friendly gear" — a second activation of any gear ability that costs its own exhaust, and a free detach if the gear is an Equipment. It is not a per-turn engine: 466.5 only establishes Control over a battlefield you did not already control and 466.5.d is what makes that a Conquer, so it pays once per change of hands, not once per turn. Same limit as the other rule of this family: 415.1 marks an object on the board, so the four gear that kill or give away their own source are left out.

synergies.name: Royal Entourage gives your legend a second activation
synergies.why: "When you play me, ready or exhaust a legend." A legend is not at a location (107.4.b) but it is on the board — 107.4.c calls the Champion Legend here a Game Object — and 415.1 readies non-spell Game Objects on the board, so the ready reaches it. The partner is your own legend: 24 of the pool's legends carry an ability with exhaust in its cost, and for those this is a second use of it per copy of Royal Entourage played. The other half of the text is the mirror, exhausting an opponent's legend before they use theirs. Five of the twenty-four charge a Disempower or an XP cost on top of the exhaust, so the second activation still has to be funded.

synergies.name: Hall of Legends readies your legend on a conquer
synergies.why: "When you conquer here, you may pay 1 Energy to ready your legend." 107.4.c makes the Champion Legend a Game Object and 415.1 readies Game Objects on the board, so a legend ability with exhaust in its cost runs twice on the turn you take this battlefield. It costs one of your three battlefield slots and only one of the three is used (485.4.a), and 466.5 / 466.5.d mean it pays on establishing Control, not on holding. Five of the twenty-four charge a Disempower or an XP cost on top of the exhaust, so the second activation still has to be funded.

synergies.name: Miss Fortune, Captain readies your legend every turn for free
synergies.why: "The first time I move each turn, you may ready something else that's exhausted" — the pool's only ready with no restriction on what it readies, and the cost is a Standard Move she was going to make anyway (144.2). 107.4.c makes the Champion Legend a Game Object and 415.1 readies Game Objects on the board, so it reaches your legend, every turn, for nothing. This does not contradict the finding that a legend is not at a location (107.4.b): the board and a location are not the same thing. Her text has no type restriction either, so the same free ready also reaches a gear or a unit when the legend does not want it. Five of the twenty-four charge a Disempower or an XP cost on top of the exhaust, so the second activation still has to be funded.

synergies.name: Stare Down empties the garrison and the battlefield is conquered without damage

excludes.why: the conquer text is quoted inside the spell and granted to the unit it moved; it is not a conquer effect Stare Down's controller has.
"you must recycle one of your runes" is a cost the conquer charges you, not a payoff it pays out; the rule pairs Stare Down with what conquering earns.

synergies.why: Send every enemy unit under your chosen unit's Might home for 2 Energy, then walk in. 190.3.a.1 and 450 make the destination Contested, 323.9 stages no Combat because no opposing units are present, 348.2.a establishes Control when the showdown closes and 348.2.a.1 says outright that this results in a Conquer. Every conquer effect you have then pays out, with no damage dealt in either direction. That is also why the list drops the ones keyed to excess damage or to conquering after an attack: with no garrison there is no Attacker designation and no Combat Damage Step (465.1), so those conditions are never met and 383.4.g.1 keeps the ability off the chain. Emptying a battlefield the opponent controls does not strip their Control by itself — 190.4.c only does that at the following cleanup — but establishing Control by walking in does.

synergies.name: Blast Cone stuns whatever else moves an enemy body
synergies.why: "When you move an enemy unit, you may exhaust this to [Stun] it" — Blast Cone charges nothing for the stun beyond its own exhaust, so it is one free stun per turn on top of any card in this list. Nothing here is a stun engine: 423.1.a.1 says a Stunned Unit cannot be Stunned again and 423.1.a.2 only clears the state at step 3d of the end of turn cleanup, so the ceiling is how many unstunned bodies the opponent has. Six of the nineteen send the body to its base, and there 423.1.b prevents no damage it was going to deal that turn — the stun is then worth only the triggers it fires, which is what makes Radiant Dawn the other half of this lens.

synergies.name: Radiant Dawn turns every stun into a buff

excludes.why: it does not stun anything — "When you stun an enemy unit, ready me" is a second payoff for the stun, so it wants the same third card Radiant Dawn does rather than pairing with her. It is also 423.1.a.1's own worked example.
same shape — "When you [Stun] an enemy unit at a battlefield, you may move me there" pays for a stun somebody else provides; she is not a source.

synergies.why: "When you stun one or more enemy units, buff a friendly unit" — she is the pool's only legend that pays for the stun, and being Calm/Order her identity reaches 21 of the pool's 29 stun lines. Buffs are where the value lands, so the cards that spend one are the follow-up, but five of the pool's seven buff spenders are Body and Domain Identity (103.1.b) keeps them out of her list on its own; the Body end of that axis is the `wallop-buff-spend` rule instead. The pool's two other stun payoffs, Eclipse Herald and Vex, Mocking, are left out for the same reason: they want the third card she wants, they do not supply it. Read "one or more" literally: she pays once per stun resolution, not once per body, and 423.1.a.1 caps the whole family — a Stunned Unit cannot be Stunned again, and 423.1.a.2 only clears the state at the end of turn cleanup.

synergies.name: Twilight Reveler's ready buys a [Ganking] body its second Standard Move
synergies.why: [Ganking] is not an extra move. 810.1.c.3 says it outright — "It does not give additional abilities or activations of Movement, only new options for the Standard Move" — and 144.4.c.1 is the only new option: battlefield to battlefield. The Standard Move's cost is exhausting the unit (420.3.a), so a body that already moved this turn needs a ready before it can move again, and that is the whole pairing. "When I attack, ready another friendly unit" costs no card and repeats on every attack, which makes it the cheapest second move in the pool: the catalogue's other multi-move lines buy theirs with effect moves that cost Energy and a card each time. What the second move is worth is the partner's business — a move trigger fires again (Jhin, Murderous Artist; Nilah, Joyful Ascetic), Kayn, Unleashed asks for two moves by name, Yasuo, Windrider scores a point on his third, and Kai'Sa, Evolutionary pays on the conquer. The tightest instance is Jayce, Hammer in Hand, whose "When I become ready, choose one to give me this turn" hands him [Ganking] with the same ready that pays for the move. The conquer is why the pattern matters at all: landing on an uncontrolled battlefield establishes Control and 348.2.a.1 makes that a Conquer, 470 caps scoring at once per battlefield per turn, and 471.1.b.1 gives the Final Point through a Conquer only to a player who has Scored every Battlefield this turn — so at 7 points one body reaching the second battlefield is the win condition, not a bonus. Three caveats the list cannot carry: the Reveler readies another unit and never itself; 415.1.b makes a ready of an already-ready unit do nothing; and Windswept Hillock and Shurelya's Requiem grant [Ganking] only "here", which pays for the one move out and not for the trip back. The Reveler must attack to pay, so a garrison has to be there — UNL-009 Upstage Comedy is the paid alternative that needs no combat and, with [Repeat], the only single card that buys Yasuo his third move.

synergies.name: On the Hunt readies the garrison, so every [Ganking] body moves twice
synergies.why: "Ready your units" for 1 Energy and 2 Power is the pool's cheapest mass ready, and against [Ganking] it converts into moves one for one: 810.1.c.3 gives no extra activation of Movement, only the battlefield-to-battlefield option of 144.4.c.1, and 420.3.a charges the Standard Move an exhaust, so each body readied is one more battlefield it can reach. It is the only one of the three ready anchors that scales with board width — a garrison of three Ganking bodies gets three second moves off one card — and it also refreshes the units that stayed home, which is what pays for a defence after the attackers have walked away. A second landing on an uncontrolled battlefield establishes Control and Conquers (348.2.a.1); 470 allows one score per battlefield per turn, so the second body has to go somewhere new, and 471.1.b.1 makes exactly that the requirement for the Final Point — a Conquer at 7 points scores only if every Battlefield was Scored that turn. Two limits: it readies units and nothing else, so the gear-borne grants in this list (Boots of Swiftness, Shurelya's Requiem) are not refreshed by it, and 415.1.b makes readying an already-ready body a no-op.

synergies.name: Acceleration Gate readies four, and the runes among them refund it
synergies.why: "Ready up to 4 units, gear, and/or runes" is the only ready in the pool that crosses all three object kinds, and that is what makes it cheap rather than merely wide: 164.2.a gives every Basic Rune "[E]: [Reaction] — Add [1]", so each rune it readies hands back an Energy and the card's own 3 Energy is largely refunded before the moves are paid for. Against [Ganking] the unit half works like the other two anchors — 810.1.c.3 grants no extra Movement activation, only 144.4.c.1's battlefield-to-battlefield option, and 420.3.a prices the Standard Move at an exhaust, so a ready is exactly one more battlefield reached; landing on an uncontrolled one establishes Control and Conquers (348.2.a.1), 470 permits one score per battlefield per turn, and 471.1.b.1 makes reaching every Battlefield in the turn the condition of the Final Point. The gear half is the part the other two anchors cannot do: it re-readies an exhausted converter, which is the third card the `ancient-henge-energy-surplus` and `hextech-anomaly-power-surplus` rules ask for. 415.1.b caps all of it — readying something already ready does nothing.

synergies.name: Ancient Henge spends surplus Energy as Power of any Domain

excludes.why: "[Add] :rb_energy_2:. Use only to play spells." — the Henge is a gear's activated ability, not a spell, so this Energy can never reach it.

"Spend this Energy only to play units or activated abilities of units" — the Henge is gear, so its ability is out of scope. Her ability also costs 2 rainbow Power to make 2 Energy, which runs the Henge's trade backwards.

synergies.why: ":rb_exhaust:: [Reaction] — Pay any amount of Energy to [Add] that much :rb_rune_rainbow:", with no cap per activation. 168 makes every [Add] ability an addition to the Rune Pool, and 135.2.e.5.b makes rainbow Power spendable on a Power cost of any Domain, so the Henge is the pool's one-way valve out of the cheap currency into the scarce one — the reason `gemdragon-henge-vi-blind-fury` keeps an Energy-only ledger. What it does not do is store: 167 empties every Rune Pool at the start of each Main Phase and at the end of each turn and 167.1 loses "any unspent Energy or Power", so the trade moves a surplus sideways inside one turn and never banks it for the next. The exhaust in its cost caps it at one conversion per turn unless the Henge is readied or replayed, which is why a ready — `acceleration-gate-ganking-second-move` readies gear — is its natural third card. Read the spend restrictions before counting a source: two of the fifteen are excluded below because their Energy is locked away from a gear ability, while Scorn of the Moon's "only during showdowns" does work, since the Henge is a [Reaction]. Chem-Baroness only adds Energy while your score is within 3 of the Victory Score, Undertitan only as it is revealed from your deck, and Threshold of the Gray pays the opponent the same 1 Energy it pays you. SFD-083 Hextech Anomaly is the mirror card rather than a source: running both converts domain-locked Power into any-domain Power (135.2.e.5.a going in, 135.2.e.5.b coming out) for two exhausts and no net resources.

synergies.name: Hextech Anomaly spends surplus Power as Energy

excludes.why: "[Add] :rb_rune_rainbow:. Use only to play spells." — the Anomaly is a gear's activated ability, so this Power can never pay it. Fire Below the Mountain is the same sentence with the opposite scope and stays in.

synergies.why: ":rb_exhaust:: [Reaction] — Pay any amount of :rb_rune_rainbow: to [Add] that much Energy" — the mirror of the Ancient Henge, uncapped in the same way, and 168 makes both of them additions to the Rune Pool. Its best partners are the six Seals, one per domain and the pool's only repeatable per-turn Power faucets: their Power is domain-locked, but 135.2.e.5.a lets a rainbow COST be paid by Power of any Domain, so a Seal of Rage reaches a Mind gear's ability without trouble. Fire Below the Mountain is the tightest fit in the list — "Use only to play gear or use gear abilities" names exactly what the Anomaly is — while Daughter of the Void prints the same restriction scoped to spells and is excluded. Four of the sixteen do not add Power in their own text at all: Bloodharbor Ripper, Deadly Flourish, Pyke, Returned and Yeti Brawler each play a Gold gear token whose quoted ability is "Kill this, :rb_exhaust:: [Add] :rb_rune_rainbow:", so they are one-shots that consume the token, not faucets. They stay in because the Power does land in your pool and the Gold token itself is never in a decklist. As with the Henge, 167 and 167.1 empty the pool at the start of every Main Phase and at the end of every turn, so this converts a surplus within the turn and stores nothing, and the exhaust in the cost allows one conversion per turn unless the Anomaly is readied.

synergies.name: Blade Dancer readies whatever a buff chooses

excludes.why: "Ready a unit" — the fragment caught is "spend a buff as an additional cost". Wallop places no buff, so 702.2.a's choose never happens; it also readies, which is the job Blade Dancer is here to do.
same sentence as Wallop — it SPENDS a buff, it does not place one. Its "Give a unit +3 Might" does choose under 355.7, but that is a different fact than the one this rule stands on.
"When you buff a friendly unit, you may pay Body Power and exhaust this to ready it" — it reacts to a buff instead of placing one, and it readies the same unit Blade Dancer would.
"When you buff me, ready me" — the same shape: a second payoff for somebody else's buff, competing with Blade Dancer for it rather than feeding her.

synergies.why: 702.2.a — "To Buff a Unit, a player CHOOSES a Unit and then places a buff on it." — so every buff in this list is a choose of a friendly unit, and Blade Dancer's "When you choose a friendly unit, you may exhaust me and pay [A] to ready it" fires on all of them. A mass buffer is several chooses off one card: Peak Guardian buffs every friendly unit at its battlefield, Fae Dragon up to four, Overt Operation all of them, Kinkou Monk two. Two limits the list cannot show. Her cost is exhausting herself, so it is one ready per turn unless something readies her — her own second line does, "When you conquer, you may pay 1 Energy to ready me". And 702.3.a means a buff aimed at a unit that already has one "is not placed instead"; the choose still happened, but a mass buffer run twice into the same board buys nothing new. Blade Dancer is Calm/Chaos and most of the mass buffers here are Body and Order, so 103.1.b keeps them apart in a real deck — the pairs this rule reaches under her are the Calm ones.

synergies.name: Irelia, Fervent grows every time a buff picks her

excludes.why: "Ready a unit" — caught by "spend a buff as an additional cost". It places no buff at all.
spends a buff instead of placing one, same sentence as Wallop.
reacts to a buff by readying the unit; it places none of its own.
its own text buffs only itself — the fragment caught is the reminder "To buff a unit, give it a +1 Might buff", a nested quote, not an instruction that can pick Irelia.
"Spend 2 XP: [Buff] me" — it can only ever choose itself, so it never reaches Irelia.
"Spend 2 XP: [Buff] me" — same, a self-buff that cannot pick another unit.

synergies.why: "When you choose or ready me, give me +1 Might this turn" and 702.2.a make a buff a choose, so each of these adds +1 Might on top of the buff's own +1 (703) — a buff aimed at Irelia is worth 2 Might the turn it lands. The predicate drops every "buff me" card on purpose: a card that can only buff itself never chooses Irelia. Two rows carry a condition the list cannot show — Arena Bar buffs an EXHAUSTED friendly unit, and Navori Fighting Pit buffs a unit HERE, so Irelia has to be standing at it. And 702.3 caps her at one buff at a time, so the repeatable half of this is the +1 Might this turn, not a stack of counters. Her [Deflect] charges an opponent a rainbow to choose her, which does not touch your own buffs.

synergies.name: Jae Medarda draws a card every time a spell picks him

excludes.why: "Give your Mechs +1 Might this turn" — Jae Medarda is tagged Noxus, not Mech, so this spell can never choose him.

"Choose a friendly unit without [Temporary]. Give it [Temporary]" — it does choose him, and then kills him at the start of your next Beginning Phase (816.1.b). Trading a 5-Might body for one card is a drawback, not a pairing.

synergies.why: "When you choose me with a spell, draw 1" — and 355.7 makes choosing a specific Game Object a target, so every spell in this list that can be pointed at a friendly unit pays a card for being pointed at Jae. Only spells are here, because his trigger names one; an ability that buffs him is worth nothing. Three shapes make the list: an explicit "Choose a friendly unit", a "+N Might" (which chooses under 355.7 even when the card never says the word), and a buff (702.2.a). Wallop is in the list on the strength of a fragment about spending a buff, and it belongs anyway — its "Ready a unit" chooses him too. The rows that damage what they choose (Challenge, Rampage, Gentlemen's Duel, Stormbringer) are kept because they are ordinary plays with a real choose, and the card they draw is the point; the two rows that only harm what they pick are excluded above.

synergies.name: Renekton, Brute buys a relative Might gate at 1 Energy per point

excludes.why: "an enemy unit here with less Might than ME" — the threshold is Imposing Challenger's own Might, and Renekton's ability only pumps Renekton.
"kill an enemy unit here with less Might than ME" — same, the gate reads Ambessa's Might, not a unit you choose.
"if it has less Might than ME" — Soraka's shield is measured against Soraka, so pumping Renekton widens nothing.
"Your units here with less Might than ME can't be chosen" — Alpha Wildclaw's own Might is the bar.
"Enemy units here with less Might than ME don't deal combat damage" — Vilemaw's own Might is the bar.

synergies.why: Renekton prints ":rb_energy_1:: Give me +1 Might this turn" with NO exhaust in the cost and no cap, so he converts Energy into Might one for one, as many times as you can pay. Two cards in the pool set their threshold against a unit YOU CHOOSE rather than against their own body, and those are the two this buys: Public Execution ("Choose a friendly unit. Kill an enemy unit with less Might than it") reaches a unit at the enemy BASE, which nothing else in the catalogue does, and Stare Down moves the whole garrison home for E2 and 1 XP. Against a 6-Might body Renekton needs 7, which is 3 activations: 3 Energy plus the spell. 477.3.e.1.a applies increases first, so the pump is in place when the spell reads — but 477.3.e.2.a applies decreases LAST, so a −Might played in response still wins the race and drops the gate under the target. The five rows excluded above measure against their own Might and are the other half of #97's inventory of 22 gates; the fixed thresholds are bought from the other side, by [[moonlight-affliction-might-gate]].

synergies.name: Moonlight Affliction collapses a fixed Might gate
synergies.why: Sixteen cards in the pool price removal by a Might threshold — kill, banish, return to hand, take control, move, or empty a garrison, all gated on "N Might or less" — and Moonlight Affliction is the largest reduction printed anywhere: "[Reaction] Give a unit -10 Might this turn", with no floor. 143.2.b is what makes it a key rather than an overpayment: "If a unit's Might is ever less than 0, it is treated as 0 WHEN REFERENCED BY SPELLS AND ABILITIES", so a body at -2 reads as 0 and contributes 0 to the four rows that gate on a TOTAL (Fox-Fire's 4, Decree of Discord's 5, Tricksy Tentacles' 8, Corrupted Dragon's per-unit 5). 143.2.b.1 is the other half: "it is not 0", so an opponent undoing it has to climb from the real number. Two limits the list cannot show. 477.3.b snapshots any "to a minimum of 1" clause at the moment it applies, so the nine Origins reductions do not stack with each other — Moonlight Affliction carries no floor, which is why it is the anchor. And 477.3.e.2.a applies decreases LAST, so the reduction always lands after the opponent's pump, whatever order the two were played in.

synergies.name: Pit Crew turns every gear you play into another Standard Move
synergies.why: "When you play a gear, ready me" is the pool's only free, uncapped ready with no cost of its own, and every gear in the list triggers it — there is nothing to read in the text, so the predicate is the card type. What the ready buys is a Standard Move: 420.3.a makes the cost of a move "Exhausting one or more Units", so an exhausted Pit Crew cannot move again until something readies it, and 415.1 is that ready. Pit Crew has no exhaust ability of its own, which is why the 2026-09-02 hunt refuted it as an engine — the ready is worth exactly one more move, and 144.4 leaves a body without [Ganking] only the round trip to its base. The gear that fixes that is itself a gear: Boots of Swiftness grants [Ganking] (144.4.c.1), and then each gear played is another battlefield-to-battlefield move, which is how a deck scores both battlefields in one turn and takes the Final Point (470, 471.1.b.1). Gold and other gear TOKENS trigger it too and are not in this list on purpose: 350.2 says "Tokens are not cards, but can still be Played", so they fire "when you play a gear" while never appearing in a decklist — and by 185 they would never fire a [Legion] or a "played a card" clause. Two independent competitive sources reached for this exact mechanism, opened directly (2026-09-06). TCGplayer, "How Did Ornn Conquer Riftbound Regional Barcelona?" (published 2026-09-02), https://www.tcgplayer.com/content/article/How-Did-Ornn-Conquer-Riftbound-Regional-Barcelona/323b4662-a8e7-4a5b-ac13-a255e339e8c2/ (read via r.jina.ai) — "For five energy, you can play Pit Crew and Brutalizer, which readies the Pit Crew and has six might when we equip it (for free thanks to Ornn!) with the Brutalizer." Issue #121 flagged the six as a printing error against a math of 3 (Pit Crew) + 2 (Brutalizer's Effect) = 5, but the article is right and #121's own arithmetic is what was short: Brutalizer carries TWO separate Might sources at once, its printed Might Bonus (137.3/137.3.a: "applied while Attached"; 477.3.d puts it in its own layer; `mightBonus: 1` in cards.json) plus its [Effect] text's conditional "additional +2 Might" for the turn it was attached — 3 + 1 + 2 = 6, confirmed against data/corpus_flat.txt and cards.json rather than corrected by assumption. And YouTube, "Riftbound | Mel Hyper Tempo!! | This List Is So Much Fun!" (uploaded 2026-09-01), https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AmHDJB7Qdrg (auto-sub read directly via yt-dlp) — "I go first, Treasure Hunter, and Pit Crew, which is a great combo" at 8:04, and "tempoing them out with Pit Crew and Call" at 45:20 (#121 placed the first quote at "~3:40"; the transcript puts it at 8:04). SFD-130 Treasure Hunter's "When I move, play a Gold gear token exhausted" is the token half of this rule's own why (350.2), played here under Mind/Chaos (Soul's Reflection) rather than Ornn's Calm/Mind — a second, independent domain pairing reaching for the same mechanism. Neither list runs Boots of Swiftness, so both stay inside the one-extra-move ceiling this why text already sets, not a bigger engine. `Synergy` carries no `sources` field (checked src/types.ts), so these two citations are recorded here rather than as structured data.

synergies.name: Shurelya's Requiem readies your units and hands out the [Ganking] itself
synergies.why: The fourth anchor of the [Ganking]-plus-ready family, and the only card that is both halves at once: "When you play this, ready your units" and "[Effect] Your units here have [Ganking]". `grep -i "ready your units"` over the corpus returns exactly two cards, this and On the Hunt, and only this one also grants the keyword. 810.1.c.3 is why the ready is what matters — [Ganking] "does not give additional abilities or activations of Movement, only new options for the Standard Move" — and 144.4.c.1 is the option itself, battlefield to battlefield. Two limits. The ready is "When you play this", not the [Equip], so Yone's and Ornn's [Weaponmaster] re-attach does not fire it again: attaching is not playing. And the [Ganking] it grants is "here", so it pays for the trip out and not for the trip back — the same caveat the other three anchors carry for Windswept Hillock. It is [Unique] (103.2.e), so a deck holds one, and Calm/Mind, an identity none of Twilight Reveler (Fury), On the Hunt (Body/Chaos) or Acceleration Gate (Mind/Body) can be played under.

synergies.name: Yordle Explorer draws off every card with two Power printed
synergies.why: "When you play a card with Power cost [A][A] or more, draw 1" — 82 cards in the pool print two or more Power, and this is the whole list. 206 is what makes it safe to read off the printed cost: "Effects that need to determine a card's cost for any purpose always use its PRINTED or copied cost, even if that cost is increased, decreased, or IGNORED as the card is played", and its own worked example is this exact clause on Lux, Illuminated. So a card played from [Hidden] for nothing (811.1.b: "you may play this, ignoring its base cost") still draws, and so does one discounted to zero. The trigger says CARD, which is the line worth knowing: 350.2 lets a token be played, and 185 says "Tokens are not cards", so no token ever draws here however much Power the thing it imitates prints. It counts an opponent's plays too — the clause is "when you play", so it does not.

synergies.name: Lady of Luminosity draws off every spell with five Energy printed
synergies.why: "When you play a spell that costs 5 Energy or more, draw 1", and 37 spells in the pool print that much. 206 settles which number is read — the PRINTED cost, "even if that cost is increased, decreased, or ignored as the card is played" — and the rule's worked example is this family: Sky Splitter costs 8 and reduces its own Energy by the highest Might you control, and it triggers Lux "regardless of how much was actually paid". Every discount in the list works the same way: Concentrate at [Level 6], Master Yi's level lines, Rhasa's own trash discount. So does [Hidden] — Hostile Takeover played face down costs 0 (811.1.b) and still counts as its printed 5. The one wording that does NOT work this way is "if you spent N or more", which reads what actually left the Rune Pool; nothing in this list is that clause. Lux, Illuminated (OGS-006) prints the same trigger for +3 Might instead of a card, on the same 37 spells.

synergies.name: Get Excited! turns an expensive card in hand into that much damage
synergies.why: "Discard 1. Deal its Energy cost as damage to a unit at a battlefield. (Ignore its Power cost.)" — the payoff IS the discarded card's cost, so the rule is a price list and the floor is where the price starts being worth a card. It is set at 7 because 7 damage kills 479 of the pool's 521 units: only 42 print 7 Might or more. 206 reads the PRINTED cost, so the best fuel is a card whose real cost is nothing like its printed one — Rhasa the Sunderer prints 10 and costs 1 less per card in your trash, Plaza Guardian prints 8 and Master Yi, Unstoppable 12. Two things the list cannot show. Get Excited! is E2 P1 Fury and 103.1.b caps the deck at the legend's two domains, so the fuel that is actually reachable is the Fury half plus one; and 422.1 makes discarding move the card "from a player's hand DIRECTLY into their trash", so every card spent here is still there for a trash payoff afterwards, which is the other half of the same lens ([[rhasa-trash-counter]]).

synergies.name: Rhasa the Sunderer gets cheaper for everything you throw away

excludes.why: "choose an OPPONENT. They [Burn 3]" — it can only ever fill somebody else's trash, and Rhasa counts YOUR trash.
"The first time I move each turn, choose a player. They [Burn 1]" — aimed at an opponent's deck; feeding your own trash with it means choosing yourself for one card a turn.
"choose a player. They discard 1" — same shape: a card written to strip an opponent's hand, not to fill your trash.

"banish your hand and trash, then [Burn 7] ... If a card would go to your trash from anywhere other than your Main Deck, banish it instead" — it empties the very counter Rhasa reads and keeps it empty. Anti-synergic, not synergic.
"you may discard 1 to return this from your trash to your hand" — one card in, one card out; the net effect on Rhasa's count is zero.

synergies.why: "I cost 1 Energy less for each card in your trash", printed at 10 Energy and 1 Power — the pool's most expensive unit and the one card that reads the trash as a resource from the paying end. 29 cards fill it, in three shapes: a discard (422.1, "moving it from a player's hand DIRECTLY into their trash"), a [Burn N] or any "put cards from your Main Deck into your trash" (431.1.b), and a look-and-keep that trashes the rest. Two facts worth carrying. The count is read when the cost is determined, so the filling has to happen first in the same turn — a discard-then-draw like Lunar Boon or Traveling Merchant is free fuel because the card comes straight back. And a Burn Out UNDOES the whole thing: 431.2.b recycles your trash into your Main Deck when you draw past the end of it, so the counter resets to zero at the exact moment a deck that has been burning itself all game runs out. This is the mirror of [[shadow-temple-trash-fuel]], which anchors on a filler and pairs it with the cards that spend the trash.

synergies.name: Startipped Peak channels a third rune a turn — one turn sooner to twelve runes, but the Empower discount it feeds arrives no sooner
synergies.why: "When you hold here, you may channel 1 rune exhausted" — 430.2 / 430.2.a make channelling the action of moving a rune off the top of the Rune Deck, readied by default unless the effect says otherwise, and its own worked example is this exact phrase, "Channel 1 rune exhausted". 315.3.b already channels 2 every Channel Phase for the Turn Player, and the Hold runs earlier in the same turn (315.2.b.2), so holding this battlefield turns the baseline into 3 runes a turn. 161.2.a caps the Rune Deck at exactly 12 cards for the whole game, so this is a ramp with a floor, not an engine: the Peak is not held before turn 3 (190.1 + 143.4), so R = 3N − 2 against the baseline 2N and the twelfth rune lands on turn 5 instead of turn 6, one turn sooner (walked in docs/phase0/walks/2026-09-06-battlefield-lens-candidates.md §3b). Exactly two cards in the pool read a rune count off the board this way — Frostcoat Mother and Grumpy Rockbear, both "[Empower] 12. This ability costs 1 Energy less for each rune you control" — so every rune this battlefield front-loads is worth 1 Energy off that Empower. It does not make the Empower land earlier: a rune is worth 1 Energy, the discount is 1 Energy per rune, and the Hold-channelled rune enters exhausted after Awaken (315.1) has already run, so it is affordable on turn 3 with or without the Peak (§3c of the same walk). What the Peak buys is headroom, one Energy per rune, from turn 4 on. Two things this is not: it is not a second engine on top of `ekko-deathknell-runes` (that entry recycles a rune already on the board; this one adds a new one from the Rune Deck) and it never restarts once the 12 are gone — 161.2.b sends a recycled rune back to the Rune Deck, but recycling is a separate action with its own cost that this Hold does not pay.

synergies.name: Reckoner's Arena pays every Hunt twice on a Hold, because 823.1.b makes it both effects at once
synergies.why: 823.1.b — "Hunt is both a Conquer and a Hold effect." — is why a Hunt keyword pays twice on the same Hold at this battlefield: once because 823.1.c.1 ("Hunt is functionally short for: When I Conquer or Hold, my controller gains X XP") already fires on any Hold, and a second time because the Arena's own text ("When you hold here, activate the conquer effects of units here") activates the SAME ability again under 383.4.g.1 — whose own worked example IS this card, reading a unit's conquer condition as fulfilled and putting the ability on the chain a second time if nothing else in its condition is unmet. `[Hunt]`, `[Hunt 2]` and `[Hunt 3]` all read the same way (823.1.c.2, c.3 — the number is just the XP value), so every one of the 13 printings in the pool doubles cleanly: the Hunt clause carries no other condition to fail 383.4.g.1's check, unlike the plain "When I conquer" cards this same anchor already excludes (Yone, Swain) on this battlefield's companion rule. `gromp-arena-svellsongur-xp` (verified) is the walked arithmetic: Voracious Gromp's [Hunt 3] pays 3 + 3 = 6 XP per Hold before Svellsongur doubles the whole thing again. One printing is not a unit at all — `UNL-096 Hunter's Machete` grants [Hunt] as Effect Text, and 434.1.c appends an Equipment's Effect Text to whatever it is attached to, so it doubles for its wearer exactly like a printed Hunt would.

synergies.name: A mass buffer banks several free Calls to Glory in one shot
synergies.why: Call to Glory only needs ONE buff — "you may spend a buff as an additional cost. If you do, ignore this spell's cost" — so any single buff already makes it free (702.2.b). What a mass buffer changes is the SUPPLY: 702.3 caps a unit at one buff, so an ability that buffs several distinct units in one resolution (Kinkou Monk up to two, Peak Guardian itself plus every other friendly unit at its battlefield, Overt Operation and Fae Dragon up to four/all) puts several spendable buffs on the board at once instead of the usual one-buff-at-a-time a card like `wallop-buff-spend` reads off the same list. 103.2.b caps Call to Glory at 3 copies, and a bank of 3+ buffs lets you cast all of them free across a turn instead of drawing into one buff per turn. 702.2.b.2 ("a player can only spend buffs on units they control") is why `Enthusiastic Promoter`'s "[Buff] all units here" — the one entry on this list with no "friendly" in its text — still banks a buff for you only from whichever of those units are yours; an enemy sharing the battlefield gets buffed too, but that buff is never yours to spend.

synergies.name: Albus Ferros turns a whole mass buff into channelled runes on one play
synergies.why: "When you play me, spend any number of buffs. For each buff spent, channel 1 rune exhausted." reads the board once, at the moment Albus enters, so its whole value is however many DIFFERENT units are already buffed then — and 702.3 ("There can only be one Buff on a Unit at a time") is exactly what makes "number of buffed units" and "number of buffs" the same count. A mass buffer played the same turn, before Albus, converts one activation into several buffed bodies and therefore several exhausted-rune channels off one ETB, instead of the one buff a turn a single-target buffer would have left on the board. 702.2.b.1 ("a buff cannot be spent from a Unit that does not have a buff") and 702.2.b.2 (only your own units) both cap the count at real, already-placed, controlled buffs — Enthusiastic Promoter's ungated "[Buff] all units here" only contributes the friendly units among them. None of the five needs sequencing beyond "resolve before Albus enters": nothing here is a Reaction that could jump the play trigger.

synergies.name: Sett, Kingpin turns a mass buff at his own battlefield into that many Might
synergies.why: "[Tank] I get +1 Might for each buffed friendly unit at my battlefield" is a continuous count, not a trigger, so it reads however many buffed bodies are standing with him at the moment combat or an ability checks it — and 702.3 ("one Buff on a Unit at a time") is the reason it never overshoots: a mass buffer run twice into the same board buys Sett nothing more, since 702.3.a refuses the second buff on a unit that already has one. Three of the five buff several units WITHOUT a location restriction (Kinkou Monk, Overt Operation, Fae Dragon), so you choose the ones standing with Sett; two are scoped to a location instead — Peak Guardian buffs "all other friendly units" only if it is itself at a battlefield, and Enthusiastic Promoter's Hold buffs only "units here" — so both of those only feed Sett when they land at HIS battlefield, not anywhere else on the board. And this does not turn into a free army: 355.2.a sends a newly created token to the controller's base or a battlefield the controller already holds, so stacking bodies specifically at Sett's battlefield is the walk measured in `docs/phase0/walks/2026-09-06-token-lens-candidates.md` (#48) — only `SFD-177 Azir, Sovereign` moves token units there in bulk, everything else is a Standard Move at a time.

synergies.name: Poro Herder buffs off any other Poro on the board
synergies.why: "When you play me, if you control a Poro, buff me and draw 1" reads the tag alone (133.8: Tags carry no innate rules meaning of their own, only what a card's own text gives them; 133.8.a says the same). Poro Herder himself carries no Poro tag ([Tags: Freljord]), so the condition needs a second, real Poro already on the board when he is played — any of the pool's other 13 Poro-tagged printings qualifies, he does not count himself.

synergies.name: Herald of Scales discounts every Dragon in the list
synergies.why: "Your Dragons' Energy costs are reduced by 2, to a minimum of 1" reads the Dragon tag off every unit that carries it (133.8/133.8.a), with no further condition — Herald of Scales is itself Mount Targon, not Dragon, so he never discounts himself. `gemdragon-henge-vi-blind-fury` already runs him alongside Gentle Gemdragon for exactly this discount; this rule generalises the pairing to all 19 Dragon-tagged printings in the pool, most of which cost 7 or more Energy and feel the discount hardest.

synergies.name: Gentle Gemdragon readies runes off every Dragon played after it
synergies.why: "When you play me or another Dragon, ready up to 2 runes" fires once for its own ETB and again every time a Dragon-tagged card is played afterward — the tag is read with no other condition (133.8/133.8.a). `gemdragon-henge-vi-blind-fury` already plays it alongside Herald of Scales' discount; this rule generalises the partner to all 19 Dragon-tagged printings, so any second Dragon played the same turn readies more runes on top of the one Gentle Gemdragon's own play already granted.

synergies.name: Direwing enters ready off any other Dragon you already control
synergies.why: "I enter ready if you control another Dragon" is checked at the moment Direwing is played, and 143.4 (units otherwise enter the Board exhausted) is exactly the default this line overrides — an Attacker or Defender designation, or a Standard Move, needs a ready unit, so landing an already-ready 7 Might body needs one of the pool's other 18 Dragon-tagged printings on the board first. Direwing carries the Dragon tag himself, so a second copy of him also satisfies a third copy's condition, but the predicate reports every OTHER Dragon printing, not the second copy of himself.

synergies.name: Friendship buffs up to +4 Might off the Bird/Cat/Dog/Poro package
synergies.why: "Give it +1 Might this turn for each of the following tags among your units — Bird, Cat, Dog, and Poro" counts DISTINCT TAGS present among your units, not copies, so it reads at most +4 no matter how many of the 59 tag-carrying printings are out — one of each of the four tags is already the cap. 133.8/133.8.a is why the tag alone (no other text) is what the card reads.

synergies.name: Stalking Wolf needs a Bird, Cat, Dog or Poro to sacrifice
synergies.why: "As an additional cost to play me, kill a Bird, Cat, Dog, or Poro you control" carries no "may" — 356.2.a.1 makes this a MANDATORY additional cost, so Stalking Wolf is literally unplayable without one of the four tags already on the board. `stalking-wolf-bird-ambush` (verified) already checked this card by card against the corpus; this rule generalises the fuel to all 59 tag-carrying printings instead of the one engine piece that entry names.

synergies.name: Starhound returns a Bird, Cat, Dog or Poro from the trash
synergies.why: "When you play me, return a Bird, Cat, Dog, or Poro from your trash to your hand" only ever finds a real printing there: 185 ("Tokens are not cards") plus 186.1 mean a token unit never remains in the trash to be chosen, so every one of the 59 tag-carrying candidates this rule lists is a genuine card the ability can actually retrieve, never a token from the family's own Bird/Deflect tokens.

synergies.name: Undying Loyalty discounts and fetches off the same four tags
synergies.why: "This costs 2 Energy less if you choose a Bird, Cat, Dog, or Poro. Play a unit with cost no more than 2 Energy and no more than 1 rainbow from your trash, ignoring its cost" reads the tag for the discount off the 59-card list this rule matches, but the caveat the list cannot show: the chosen unit ALSO has to fit the printed cost cap to be the thing actually played from the trash, which narrows the real target list to the cheap end of it.

synergies.name: Ivern, Friend to All scores off holding all four tags
synergies.why: "As you play me, choose Bird, Cat, Dog, or Poro. I gain that tag. When I conquer or hold, score 1 point if your units have all of the following tags among them" supplies one of the four tags himself, so only the remaining three need to come from the 59-card list this rule matches. `ivern-sentinel-hold` and `ivern-arena-sentinel-hold` are both verified combos built on exactly this condition, multiplied by Blue Sentinel or Reckoner's Arena; this rule is the general pattern those two entries hand-walked one board each.

synergies.name: Daisy! gets cheaper and stuns off the same four tags
synergies.why: "I enter ready. Reduce my cost by 1 Energy for each of the following tags among your units — Bird, Cat, Dog, and Poro. When I attack while your units have all 4 tags, Stun an enemy unit here" counts distinct tags the same way Friendship and Ivern, Friend to All do, off the same 59-card list, discounting up to 4 Energy off her printed 9 and unlocking the free Stun attack trigger only once all four are represented.

synergies.name: Green Father turns a battlefield into a permanent Might bonus for the four-tag package
synergies.why: "When you conquer or hold, you may exhaust me to replace that battlefield with a Brush battlefield token. Bird, Cat, Dog, Poro, and Ivern units have +1 Might in Brush" is the standard conquer-or-hold wording (383.4.c.1, 383.4.d.1) gating a one-shot Effect that then grants a permanent, location-locked Might bonus to the same package Friendship and Ivern, Friend to All read, plus the Ivern champion tag itself — 133.8/133.8.a is why the tag alone drives it. The bonus is scoped to whichever battlefield became Brush, not the whole board.

synergies.name: Grim Resolve pays 2 XP off any of the [Action] spells that empty a Combat's other side

partner.textMatches: \[Action\][\s\S]*?(unit at a battlefield|Mights? to each other|Deal \d+ to an enemy|[Mm]ove .*? from a battlefield)

excludes.why: Zenith Blade only stuns. 423.1.b removes a Stunned unit's contribution to Combat Damage, it does not remove the unit from the battlefield, so 465.1's 'if both Attacking and Defending units remain' gate is still met and the Damage Step still runs — this spell never empties a side the way a kill/banish/bounce/steal/move does.

[BANNED constructed:banned, 2v2:banned]. Fight or Flight moves the targeted unit to its base, exactly the shape this rule is built on, but Riot has already banned it in both formats, so it can never actually pair with Grim Resolve in a legal deck.

synergies.why: Grim Resolve's own payoff — "Give a friendly unit +3 Might this turn. When it wins a combat this turn, gain 2 XP." — is a plain won-a-combat trigger, indifferent to how the other side emptied. Buff a unit on either side of a Combat, then clear the OTHER side's whole garrison with one of these [Action] spells (an outright Kill, lethal damage, a bounce, a banish, a steal-and-recall, a deck-return, or a move to base): 465.1's "if both Attacking and Defending units remain at this battlefield" gate fails, 465.3 skips the Damage Step, and 466.3.a hands the win — and the XP — to whoever is left standing. This fires whether the removal comes from the Attacker clearing the Defender (the shape sinister-poro-attack-evacuate walks, at 1 Energy with no spell at all) or from the Defender clearing the Attacker inside the Showdown the opponent's own attack opened, which only 806.1.b's off-turn permission reaches (possession-action-defender-flip). Two spells in the family price the buff's own domain out: Blast of Power (Order) and Keeper's Verdict/Zenith Blade's cousins in Body/Order/Calm are outside Grim Resolve's mono-Body identity unless the legend also carries that domain.

synergies.name: Pyke, Returned only pays off the members of the family that actually kill

partner.textMatches: \[Action\][\s\S]*?(unit at a battlefield|Mights? to each other|Deal \d+ to an enemy|[Mm]ove .*? from a battlefield)

excludes.why: Zenith Blade only stuns; the unit is never removed from the battlefield at all, let alone killed (423.1.b).
[BANNED constructed:banned, 2v2:banned]. Fight or Flight moves the unit to its base — never a Kill, so it would not pay Pyke even if it were legal.
Rebuke returns the unit to its owner's hand. It never reaches the Trash, so 428.1's "going to the trash from the board" is never satisfied and the unit never dies.
Possession takes control and Recalls the unit to the controller's own base (455/456). A Recall is explicitly not a Kill and the unit stays on the board the whole time, so it never dies.

Smite's own text replaces the death outright — "If it would die this turn, banish it instead" — so whenever the damage would be lethal the unit is banished, never sent to the Trash, and it never dies.
Keeper's Verdict places the unit on the top or bottom of its owner's Main Deck. It leaves the board without ever reaching the Trash, so it never dies.
Wind and Ghosts either banishes (3 Might or less) or returns the unit to its owner's hand. Neither branch sends it to the Trash, so it never dies.

synergies.why: "Once each turn, when an enemy unit dies while I'm at a battlefield, play a Gold gear token exhausted" keys on an actual death, and 428.1 defines Killing as a Permanent going to the Trash from the board. 808.1.d and 808.1.d.1 — written for Deathknell, but stating the same event — say outright that when a "killed" event is replaced by anything else (their own worked example is a recall), the death never happened and the trigger is stripped from the chain before it fires. So Pyke only pairs with the members of this family that actually put the enemy in the Trash: the damage-based removal spells (including the two mutual-damage spells, which can kill the enemy side of the exchange) and the two unconditional Kill instructions. The bounce, the steal-and-recall, the deck-return, the banish-or-bounce and the banish-that-replaces-death all empty the battlefield just as well for the ENGINE this family already stands on (possession-action-defender-flip, sinister-poro-attack-evacuate), but none of them ever pays Pyke.

synergies.name: Portal Rescue replays a body for free, off the board instead of out of hand

excludes.why: the predicate caught "play a non-token gear" in his trigger condition; his play effect readies something, it puts nothing on the board.
